deep.reconstruction:
Setting (as on the page): α, β, γ are complex numbers for the vertices of a triangle, taken 'in natural order' (the formulas require counterclockwise orientation). A, B, C are the angles at α, β, γ. u is the circumcentre.

(1) Circumcentre. The circumcentre lies on the perpendicular bisector of side αβ. It sits at distance (c/2)·cot C from the midpoint (α+β)/2. It lies on the same side as γ, which for counterclockwise order is the direction i(β−α). Hence u = (α+β)/2 + i(β−α)cot C/2, i.e.
2u = α+β+(β−α)i·cot C = α(1−i cot C) + β(1+i cot C).
The ink blots in the manuscript stand for the minus signs. Cyclically:
2u = β(1−i cot A)+γ(1+i cot A) = γ(1−i cot B)+α(1+i cot B).

(2) Centroid. 3t = α+β+γ.

(3) Orthocentre. Subtracting the cyclic forms of 2u from 3t gives:
3t−2u = α+(β−γ)i·cot A = β+(γ−α)i·cot B = γ+(α−β)i·cot C.
Gauss states that this point is where the three perpendiculars from the vertices to the opposite sides meet. (My justification, not written on the page: H−α = i(β−γ)cot A is a real multiple of i(β−γ). So H lies on the line through α perpendicular to βγ, and likewise for the other two vertices.) In modern terms this is H = 3G − 2O, i.e. H = α+β+γ when O = 0 (Euler line).

(4) Pairwise subtraction of the three expressions for 3t−2u gives three identities:
0 = α−β + i{α cot B + β cot A − γ(cot A+cot B)}, and its cyclic permutations.
Each is equivalent (my reformulation) to γ = [α(cot B − i) + β(cot A + i)]/(cot A+cot B). This is the same as (γ−α)/(β−α) = (sin B/sin C)·e^{iA}, the complex form of the law of sines plus the angle at α. So these are consistency conditions linking the vertex coordinates with the angles.

A red bracketed editorial pencil note follows, read as '[unrichtig]' (uncertain reading). The top-left mark 'IV 396' appears to be an editor's reference to Gauss, Werke Bd. IV, p. 396, i.e. the note was printed there.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All formulas are correct provided the vertices are taken counterclockwise; for clockwise order every i would change sign.
The orthocentre property of 3t−2u is asserted rather than proved, though it follows immediately from the form α+i(β−γ)cot A.

If the red editorial note reads 'unrichtig', it is not justified by the mathematics: the identities check out, both symbolically and against an equilateral example. The reading may be something else (e.g. 'unwichtig').

results.what: Complex-coordinate formula for the circumcentre: 2u = α+β+i(β−α)cot C, with cyclic variants
results.modern_name: Circumcentre in complex coordinates (complex-number triangle geometry)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard; complex-number methods in triangle geometry developed in the 19th century (e.g. Bellavitis-style vector methods, later textbook material)

results.what: Identities 0 = α−β + i{α cot B + β cot A − γ(cot A+cot B)}
results.modern_name: Complex form of the similarity/angle relation (γ−α)/(β−α) = (sin B/sin C)e^{iA}

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary triangle geometry (circumcentre, centroid, orthocentre and Euler line) written in complex coordinates. The Euler line is Euler's. Gauss's use of complex numbers for plane geometry is well known, and the 'IV 396' mark indicates the note was printed in Werke IV. Only the early systematic use of complex coordinates is mildly of interest.

checkable.asserts: 2u = α+β+i(β−α)cot C gives the circumcentre (equidistant from all three vertices) for counterclockwise vertices 0, 1, p+iq.
The three cyclic expressions for 2u agree.

checkable.asserts: 3t−2u lies on the altitudes, i.e. it is the orthocentre.
The three identities obtained by subtraction hold.

transcription_corrections: The ink blots read as '[?]' in α(1 − i cot C), β(1 − i cot A), γ(1 − i cot B) are minus signs; this is confirmed mathematically.
'IV 396' at top left is an editorial cross-reference (apparently Werke Bd. IV, p. 396), not part of Gauss's text.
The red bracketed note near the bottom is an editorial pencil mark; the reading 'unrichtig' is uncertain and does not match the (correct) mathematics.
'gegen [einander] über liegenden': 'einander' is struck through and 'über' is written above, giving 'gegenüberliegenden'.
